blocks.text: A wild wooded and rocky valley on the Rhine, which flows past a steep cliff in the background. The three Rhine-Maidens, Woglinde, Wellgunde, and Flosshilde, rise to the surface and swim and circle as if dancing.

lines: Our father’s gold shone on the billows.
How bright was once thy radiance,

blocks.text: They sing and again start swimming and circling about. They pause and listen, then merrily splash the waters.

lines: Who again our gold shall give us!
Envy thine eye for its splendour.

blocks.text: Appears on the cliff fully armed.

lines: Some elf has led me astray
And lured my feet from the path.

blocks.text: Rise to the surface again and swim and circle as in a dance.

lines: With what elf art thou so wroth?
Hast thou been tricked by some sprite?
Tell us, Siegfried; let us hear!
So ask of me what you will.
I won the ring in fight;
And think ye for a worthless bear-skin
On you did I waste my goods,
My wife would have cause to scold.
Has the hero felt her hand?
In grief ye shall be left,
Ye ask shall never be yours.

blocks.text: The Rhine-Maidens have again joined hands for dancing.

lines: How sad he should a miser be!

blocks.text: Comes down nearer to the river.

lines: The ring gladly I’d give them.
Come back; the ring shall be yours.

blocks.text: He holds up the ring, which he has taken from his finger.
Rise to the surface again. They appear grave and solemn.

lines: Until the harm thou hast felt
That in the ring lies hid.
Be freed by us from its curse.

blocks.text: Calmly puts the ring on his finger again.

lines: Wilt thou not give to the Rhine
The ring to hide in its waters.
Was I firm when ye flattered,
I am firmer now when ye threaten!
Flee, oh, flee from the curse!
My sword once shattered a spear;
But he could not teach me to fear.
Has bestowed on me a ring.
And still for love might it be got,
But by threats to my life and my limbs—
The ring ye never shall gain.

blocks.text: He lifts a clod of earth from the ground, holds it over his head, and with the last words throws it behind him.

lines: He is blind and in fetters bound fast.

blocks.text: Wildly excited, they swim in wide circles close to the shore.

lines: And was false to his word;
And the ring that deals doom and death
Ere night falls thy wealth shall inherit.
Our cry by her will be heard.
To her! To her! To her!

blocks.text: They turn quickly to their dance, and gradually swim away to the back singing.
Looks after them smiling, one foot on a piece of rock and his chin resting on his hand.

lines: Still those who mistrust their smiles
They seek with threats to frighten,
At once they begin to scold.

blocks.text: He looks calmly after the Rhine-Maidens, who have disappeared, and whose voices gradually die away. Horn-calls are then heard. Siegfried starts from a reverie and sounds his horn in answer.
Having first answered the call with his horn.
Appears on the height, followed by Gunther. He sees Siegfried.

lines: Come down all! Here ’tis fresh and cool.

blocks.text: The vassals now appear on the height, and come down with Hagen and Gunther.
They lay the game in a heap.
Wine-skins and drinking-horns are produced. All lie down.

lines: Now be the wonders told us
That chased the game from us.
No meal at all is mine;
To share with me your spoil.
A brood of three wild water-birds
I had caught and brought you.
Down there on the Rhine they told me
That slain to-day I should fall.

blocks.text: Gunther starts and looks darkly at Hagen. Siegfried lies down between Gunther and Hagen.
Whilst he orders a drinking-horn to be filled for Siegfried, and hands it to him.

lines: That thou canst tell the meaning

blocks.text: He takes the drinking-horn and turns with it to Gunther, to whom he offers it after he has drunk from it.
Looks into the horn with horror. Moodily.

lines: A pale draught thou hast poured!
With thine, then, be it mingled!

blocks.text: He pours from Gunther’s horn into his own so that it runs over.

lines: Thus mixed the wine flows over
May it prove a cordial kind!
She speaks less plain to him
Than speak the birds to thee!
Since I have heard women singing.
The birds I have clean forgot.
But thou didst hear them once?
If thou wouldst care to hear them.

blocks.text: All lie down close to Siegfried, who alone sits upright.

lines: He might slay a dragon grim
That guarded treasure in the wood.
Out of the splinters of a weapon
The wood then we sought, and there
I have marvels to tell you.
And these I raised to my lips;
Was the blood by my tongue,
When what a bird was saying
On a bough it sat there and sang:
Tarnhelm, if he could but win it,
Would help him to deeds of renown;
And could he discover the ring,
It would make him the lord of the world!”
Was that the end of the singing?
He sat above me and sang:—
Both the helm and the ring!
For Mime, too, covets the treasure,
He is bent on murdering Siegfried;
The steel that he forged not

blocks.text: He has another drinking-horn filled, and drops the juice of a herb into it.

lines: What further did the bird tell thee?
It will mind thee of things long forgotten,
And bring old days to remembrance.

blocks.text: He offers the horn to Siegfried, who looks into it thoughtfully and then drinks slowly.

lines: He sat there still and sang.
She sleeps where rugged rocks soar;
Ringed is her chamber by fire.
Till I came to the fire-ringed rock.
Sleeping, and clad in bright mail,
And waked the maid with my kiss.
Ah, then the burning, sweet embrace

blocks.text: Springing up in the greatest consternation.
Two ravens fly up out of a bush, circle above Siegfried, and then fly away towards the Rhine.
Siegfried starts up suddenly, and, turning his back to Hagen, looks after the ravens. Hagen thrusts his spear into Siegfried’s back.

Gunther and the vassals rush towards Hagen. Siegfried swings his shield on high with both hands in order to throw it on Hagen; his strength fails him; the shield drops from his grasp backwards, and he falls down upon it.
Who have tried to hold Hagen back in vain.
He turns calmly away, and is seen in the gathering twilight disappearing slowly over the height. Gunther bends over Siegfried in great grief. The vassals stand round the dying man full of sympathy.
Supported by two vassals in a sitting posture, opens radiant eyes.

lines: And bound thee in slumber so fast?

blocks.text: He sinks back and dies. The rest stand round him motionless and sorrowing. Night has fallen. At a silent command from Gunther the vassals raise Siegfried’s body and bear it away slowly in a solemn procession over the height. The moon breaks through the clouds, and lights up the funeral procession with increasing clearness as it reaches the top of the hill. A mist has risen from the Rhine which gradually fills the whole stage, on which the funeral procession has become invisible. After a musical interlude the mist divides again, until at length the hall of the Gibichungs, as in Act I. appears with increasing distinctness.
It is night. The moonlight is mirrored in the Rhine. Gutrune comes out of her chamber into the hall.

lines: I saw go down to the shore?

blocks.text: She listens at the door at the right and calls.
She opens the door timidly and looks into the inner room.

lines: I saw go downwards to the Rhine.

blocks.text: Hagen’s voice is heard outside coming nearer. When Gutrune hears it she stands for a time transfixed with terror.
Increasing light from the torches is seen without. Hagen enters the hall.
Men and women with lights and firebrands accompany, in great confusion, the procession returning with Siegfried’s body.

lines: Or gaily go wooing fair women.

blocks.text: The procession reaches the middle of the hall, and the vassals set down the body on a hastily improvised platform.

lines: ’Tis a wild boar’s spoil they bring thee:

blocks.text: Gutrune shrieks and falls upon the corpse. General emotion and mourning.

lines: These men have murdered my Siegfried!
Cast not the blame on me;
He is the accursèd wild boar
That did the hero to death.
With me art wroth for that?
Yes, then, ’tis true that I slew him.
By my spear he falsely swore,
So by my spear he fell.
And what I claim is this ring.
Ye vassals, judge of my right!
The Niblung son demands his own.

blocks.text: He rushes on Gunther, who defends himself: they fight. The vassals throw themselves between. Gunther falls slain by a stroke from Hagen.
He makes a grasp at Siegfried’s hand, which raises itself in menace. All stand transfixed with horror.
Advances firmly and solemnly from the background to the front. Still at the back.

lines: Now for vengeance his wife comes,
When milk is spilt by their mother;

blocks.text: Raising herself suddenly from the floor.

lines: Thou art the cause of our woe!
For, urged by thee, the men have slain him;
Cursèd hour that brought thee here!
Thou never wert wife of his;
But I am his lawful bride;
To me was the binding oath sworn,
Why didst thou give the poison
Whom through the draught he forgot.

blocks.text: She turns from Siegfried in shame and fear, and, dying, bends over Gunther’s body; remaining motionless in this position until the end. Hagen stands defiantly leaning on his spear and shield, sunk in gloomy thought, on the opposite side. Brünnhilde stands alone in the middle. After long and absorbed contemplation of Siegfried she turns with solemn exaltation to the men and women.

lines: And high by the Rhine be heaped;
Him who was first among men!
His horse lead to me here,
That with me his lord he may follow.
To have part in his glory
And share his honour in death.

blocks.text: The young men, during the following, raise a great pyre of logs before the hall, near the bank of the Rhine; women decorate this with rugs, on which they strew plants and flowers.
Absorbed anew in contemplation of Siegfried’s dead face. Her expression brightens and softens as she proceeds.

lines: Barred he lay by his sword.
That else upon thee had fallen.
That wise a woman might grow!
Know I all thou wouldst learn?
By them I send thee back
Rest in peace now, O God!

blocks.text: She signs to the vassals to bear Siegfried’s body on to the pyre; at the same time she draws the ring off Siegfried’s finger, and regards it musingly.

lines: For your counsel good, ye who dwell
In the waters deep of the Rhine.
The fire by which I am burnt
Cleanses the ring of its curse.
That stolen was to your grief!

blocks.text: She has put the ring on her finger, and now turns to the pile of logs on which Siegfried’s body lies stretched. Taking a great firebrand from one of the men, she waves it and points to the background.

lines: That ye have heard by the Rhine.

blocks.text: She hurls the brand on to the pile of wood, which quickly breaks into flame. Two ravens fly up from the rock by the shore and vanish in the background. Brünnhilde perceives her horse, which has just been led in by two men.
She springs towards him, and, catching hold of him, removes his bridle and bends towards him affectionately.

lines: To think thou shalt join him?
Have laid hold on my heart.

blocks.text: She has swung herself on to the horse, and urges it forward.

lines: See! Brünnhild’ greets thee, thy bride!

blocks.text: She urges her horse with one leap into the burning pile of logs. The flames immediately blaze up, so that they fill the whole space in front of the hall and seem to catch hold of the building itself. The terrified men and women press as far to the front as possible. When the whole stage appears to be filled with fire the glow gradually fades, so that there is soon nothing left but a cloud of smoke, which drifts towards the back and hangs there as a dark bank of cloud. At the same time the Rhine overflows and the flood rolls up over the fire. The three Rhine-Maidens swim forward on the waves, and now appear over the spot where the fire was. Hagen, who since the incident of the ring has been watching Brünnhilde’s behaviour with growing anxiety, is much alarmed by the sight of the Rhine-Maidens. He throws away his spear, shield, and helmet, and dashes into the flood as if mad, crying out, “Back from the ring!” Woglinde and Wellgunde fling their arms round his neck and, swimming away, draw him down with them into the depths. Flosshilde, swimming ahead of the others towards the back, joyously holds up the recovered ring. Through the bank of cloud on the horizon a red glow of increasing brightness breaks forth, and, illumined by this light, the Rhine-Maidens are seen merrily circling about and playing with the ring on the calmer waters of the Rhine, which has gradually retired to its natural bed. From the ruins of the fallen hall the men and women watch in great agitation the growing gleam of fire in the heavens. When this is at its brightest the hall of Walhall is seen, in which the Gods and heroes sit assembled, as described by Waltraute in the first Act. Bright flames seem to seize on the hall of the Gods. When the Gods are completely hidden by the flames the curtain falls.
